title: Open maps, homeomorphisms, and topological invariants
section: Point-Set Topology ▷ Open Maps and Homeomorphisms
terms: open map; homeomorphism; topological invariant; compact-to-Hausdorff theorem.

exposition.text:
An open map takes open subsets of its domain to open subsets of its codomain. A homeomor-
phism is a bijection whose map and inverse are both continuous; equivalently it is a continuous
open bijection. Homeomorphisms preserve properties defined by topology, including compact-
ness, connectedness, and the number of components after deleting specified points.
A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is automatically a home-
omorphism: closed domain subsets are compact, their images are compact and hence closed,
so the inverse is continuous. Without these hypotheses a continuous bijection need not be a
homeomorphism.

question.text:
A continuous bijection f : X → Y is given, where X is compact and Y is Hausdorff. Which
must be true?
(A) X is finite.
(B) Y is connected.
−1
(C) f is continuous.
(D) Y is discrete.
(E) Every subset of X is compact.

solution.text:
For any closed F ⊆ X, compactness of X makes F compact. Its image is compact in Haus-
dorff Y , hence closed. Thus f is a closed bijection and its inverse is continuous.

question.text:
Give R its usual topology and N the discrete topology. Define f : R → N by f(x) = 0 for
0 0
x ≤ 0 and f(x) = 1 for x > 0. Which statement is correct?
(A) f is continuous and open.
(B) f is continuous but not open.
(C) f is open but not continuous.
(D) f is neither open nor continuous.
(E) f is a homeomorphism.

solution.text:
The image of any open set is a subset of the discrete codomain, and every such subset is
open, so f is an open map. But the open singleton {0} has inverse image (−∞, 0], which is
not open in the domain. Thus f is not continuous; being an open map does not require a
bijection or surjectivity.

The map f : [0, 2π) → S is f (t) = (cos t, sin t), with both spaces carrying their usual subspace
1
topologies. At which points of S is the inverse function discontinuous?
(A) No points
(B) Only (−1, 0)
(C) Only (1, 0)
(D) Every point with second coordinate zero
(E) Every point

solution.text:
The map is a continuous bijection. Away from (1, 0), a local angle can be chosen continu-
ously within (0, 2π). But f(2π − 1/n) → (1, 0) = f (0), while the inverse images 2π − 1/n
do not converge to zero. Thus the inverse fails continuity exactly at (1, 0). The half-open
domain is not compact, so the compact-to-Hausdorff theorem does not apply.

question.text:
Which property is invariant under homeomorphism?
(A) Being bounded in an ambient Euclidean space
(B) Compactness
(C) Euclidean diameter
(D) Euclidean distance
(E) The numerical value of area

solution.text:
Homeomorphisms and their inverses preserve open covers, hence compactness. Bounded-
ness is not topological: the bounded interval (0, 1) is homeomorphic to the unbounded line
R.
